subtitle: The deep end: execution-plan thinking, index strategies, query rewriting, recursive CTEs, transactions, and the optimization workflow that separates seniors from scripters
audience: Developers fluent in intermediate SQL (subqueries, CTEs, set ops, CASE, views — the SQL Intermediate graduate) who now own slow queries, growing tables, and concurrent writers. Flat exploration queries run in the SQL Query Sandbox; plans, indexes, DDL, recursion, windows, and transactions target real SQLite or PostgreSQL — the sandbox teaches SELECT, and this course is explicit about where each statement runs.
outcomes: Read EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN / EXPLAIN output and trace any slow query to its dominant operation
Design composite, covering, and partial indexes with correct column order and measured justification
Rewrite queries for speed: sargability, decorrelation, OR-to-UNION surgery, keyset pagination
Write WITH RECURSIVE walks (anchor, step, termination proof) for hierarchies and sequence gaps
Rank and annotate with window functions (ROW_NUMBER/RANK/DENSE_RANK, PARTITION BY, frames) and know where the primer ends
Wrap multi-statement work atomically, choose isolation levels and locking modes, and implement retry logic
Control CTE materialization and stage expensive pipelines with temp tables deliberately
Execute full optimization rescues: baseline, rewrite, index, verify, document
Review SQL for the nine classic antipatterns with harm + fix + proof comments
Perform scoped performance audits delivering findings, guardrails, and deferred lists

assessment.q: EXPLAIN shows SCAN on a 28-row table vs the same SCAN at 28M rows. Verdicts?
options: Fine at 28 rows; prime suspect at 28M — plan nodes are scale-relative
assessment.explain: Scanning 28 rows beats index hops; scanning 28M dominates cost. Seniors judge nodes against table size (Ch.1).

assessment.q: Index on (course_id, completed). Which filter is unserved, and why?
options: completed-alone — left-prefix rule: structures open from the leftmost column
assessment.explain: Composites serve the full key and left prefixes only. Second-column-only filters need their own index or reordered composite (Ch.2).

assessment.q: WHERE UPPER(email) = 'A@X.IO' ignores the email index. Minimal correct fix?
options: Compare the normalized constant (email = 'a@x.io') or normalize at write time — bare columns seek
assessment.explain: Sargability: functions blind indexes. Move computation to the value side (Ch.3).

assessment.q: Recursive CTE hangs on production data but worked in testing. Cause + guard?
options: A data cycle defeats naive termination — carry depth/path with an explicit bound
assessment.explain: Clean test trees terminate; production cycles don't. Seatbelt every walk (Ch.4).
Arbitrary order vs shared-with-skip vs shared-dense — match tie policy to use: pagination, prizes, tiers (Ch.5).

assessment.q: Why can't WHERE rn <= 2 share a query level with its ROW_NUMBER() definition?
options: Pipeline order: windows compute after WHERE — rank inside, filter outside
assessment.explain: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → windows → SELECT → ORDER BY. Same-level WHERE predates the window (Ch.5).

assessment.q: Two writers read 5, add 1, write 6. Result, name, and cheapest sufficient fix?
options: 6, lost update — single-statement atomic UPDATE (SET n = n + 1) suffices for counters
assessment.explain: Interleaved read-modify-write loses an increment. Atomic single statements fix counters; reserve optimistic/SERIALIZABLE for richer invariants (Ch.6).

assessment.q: PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE aborts with 40001 under load. Handling?
options: Retry the idempotent unit with bounds + backoff — expected control flow
assessment.explain: Serializable safety aborts conflicts by design; the app contract is retry. Spikes coincide with load (Ch.6).

assessment.q: A 3x-referenced CTE dominates runtime though each use is cheap. Fix?
options: MATERIALIZED (PG) or temp-table staging — inlining evaluates per reference
assessment.explain: Reference count rules evaluation count under inlining. Command sharing explicitly (Ch.7).

assessment.q: First step on a slow-dashboard ticket, and why that order?
options: Reproduce + baseline (plan + timing on production-shaped data) — no baseline, no proof or attribution
assessment.explain: Every claim references the baseline. Rewrite-then-index follows, one measured arrow at a time (Ch.8).

assessment.q: Loop of 300 per-row COUNTs. Diagnosis, fix, proof?
options: N+1 call-pattern bug — batch to one GROUP BY; prove with query-log counts before/after
assessment.explain: Round trips dominate regardless of per-query speed. Batching collapses 300 to 1 (Ch.9).

assessment.q: Rollup is slow AND fanout-inflated. Order of operations?
options: Correctness first (remove/isolate fanout) — wrong fast is still wrong — then optimize the correct shape
assessment.explain: Inflated trust costs exceed latency costs. Fix shape correctness, then speed, then guardrails (Ch.10).

project.title: The Catalog Performance Audit
project.summary: You are the database owner for a growing DevPath deployment: three dashboard queries time out under load and leadership suspects the data layer. You inventory, EXPLAIN, rank by impact, rescue with rewrites and minimal indexes, verify every arrow, and deliver findings plus regression guardrails — the audit loop this course drilled, at full scale.
requirements: Suspect inventory: three slow query shapes (leaderboard with scalar + OFFSET, OR search with wildcards, fanout-inflated rollup) with baselines (plan nodes + timings on production-shaped data)
Rescue 1 — leaderboard: flattened grouped derived table + keyset pagination + plan-proven composite, with before/after plans and times
Rescue 2 — search: sargabilized predicates + UNION ALL split with disjointness guards (or justified UNION), plus a documented trigram/FTS follow-up for genuine substring needs
Rescue 3 — rollup: fanout removed (join deleted or pre-aggregated), correctness proven by row-count agreement, then optimized
Index ledger: every CREATE/DROP with the plan node that demanded it; unused-index audit of the schema with at least one deletion proposal
Guardrails: keyset-only pagination rule, sargability + N+1 review-checklist entries, and a deferred list with reasons
technical: Exploration and preservation baselines run in the SQL Query Sandbox (flat); plans, DDL, recursion, windows, and timings run in real SQLite and PostgreSQL
Each rescue ships baseline plan + timing, change, re-plan + timing — one measured arrow at a time
Rewrites preserve rows: pre/post counts recorded for every shape change
Findings cite plan nodes (SCAN/SEARCH/TEMP B-TREE), not adjectives
project.architecture: Four sections: (1) Executive summary — three suspects impact-ranked (frequency × cost) with total speedup claimed and measured; (2) Per-suspect dossiers — baseline, change, verification, guardrail; (3) Index ledger — created/dropped/kept with per-index justification; (4) Deferred + prevention — trigram follow-up, review checklist additions, and what gets re-audited next quarter.
steps: Reproduce all three suspects on production-shaped data; record baselines before touching anything
Rank by impact; attack in order with rewrite-first discipline and row-preservation counts
Add only plan-demanded indexes; re-EXPLAIN every change; confirm node transitions
Audit the existing index set; propose at least one DROP with usage evidence
Write guardrails and the deferred list; assemble the four-section deliverable
Self-review against the Ch.9 gallery: no SELECT *, no OFFSET, no bare ORs, no magic numbers in shipped SQL
evaluation: All three rescues measured end-to-end with plan transitions documented (SCAN→SEARCH or equivalent)
Row preservation proven for every rewrite; fanout eliminated with agreement counts
Index ledger justifies each create/drop from plans; at least one deletion proposed
Guardrails are enforceable rules, not advice; deferred items carry reasons
Shipped SQL passes the Ch.9 checklist visibly
stretch: Add a recursive-CTE-powered hierarchy report (e.g., topic trees) with termination proof and timing
Convert one hot dashboard source to a MATERIALIZED/temp-table stage with refresh contract and staleness guard
Benchmark covering vs plain composite on the leaderboard query and report the margin with plans

interviewQs.q: Walk me through a slow query: what do you do first, and what do you refuse to do?
interviewQs.a: First: reproduce with EXPLAIN (+ANALYZE in PG) and timing on production-shaped data — record the baseline. Refuse: adding indexes or rewriting blind, changing two things at once, and optimizing descriptions instead of measurements. Then: rewrite shape first (flatten, sargabilize, keyset), index the plan-proven remainder minimally, verify each arrow, document baselines and guardrails. The through-line is attribution — every claim traceable to a measured plan transition.

interviewQs.q: Explain sargability with three examples of killing it and fixing it.
interviewQs.a: Sargable = the engine can seek an index: bare column vs value. Killers: UPPER(col) = 'X' (fix: normalized constant or write-time normalization), col + 100 > 500 (fix: col > 400), strftime('%Y', created) = '2026' (fix: half-open range >= AND <). Each fix moves computation to the value side so the column stands naked for the index. Date ranges are the highest-value instance in practice.

interviewQs.q: When is a CTE the wrong tool, and what replaces it?
interviewQs.a: When it is expensive and referenced multiple times — inlining can evaluate it per reference. Replacements by need: MATERIALIZED (PG) to command compute-once, temp tables when the stage needs inspection/indexing/reuse across statements, and plain inlining (or a flattened join) when single-use optimization beats ceremony. Decide by reference count and EXPLAIN evidence, never by elegance.

interviewQs.q: Design the pagination for a million-row leaderboard. Why not OFFSET?
interviewQs.a: OFFSET reads-and-discards N rows (page 5000 costs 250x page 1) and drifts on concurrent writes. Keyset pagination: WHERE (sort_key, id) past the last-seen bookmark, ORDER BY, small LIMIT — constant cost, drift-immune. The id tiebreaker guarantees a unique total order so rows never skip or repeat. OFFSET survives only for tiny tables and admin screens.

interviewQs.q: Isolation levels: what do you run by default, and when do you escalate?
interviewQs.a: Defaults (READ COMMITTED / deferred locking) for ordinary work; escalate for money-like invariants — balances, seat counts, caps. REPEATABLE READ for snapshot-consistent multi-read reports; SERIALIZABLE + retry loops for multi-row invariants under contention; SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE + short transactions + WAL for writer-heavy SQLite. Escalation buys safety with latency/aborts — proportionate to the invariant's value, with retry as production code.

interviewQs.q: UNION vs UNION ALL, and the one question that decides it?
interviewQs.a: The question is 'must duplicates be removed?' — UNION dedupes via a sort/hash over the combined set (dominant cost at scale), UNION ALL stacks untouched. Default ALL; pay for UNION only when distinctness is specified. Plus the contract: equal counts, positional type compatibility, first query names output, single trailing ORDER BY — and disjointness guards when splitting ORs into ALL branches.
